sections.0.body.0.t: Tool calling (also called function calling) is the interface through which an LLM returns, instead of (or in addition to) text, a structured function call: tool name + arguments in JSON. The runtime receives it, validates the arguments against a schema, executes and returns the result to the context.

sections.0.body.1.t: The model never executes anything on its own. It only proposes: 'I would call get_weather with { city: 'São Paulo' }'. Execution, authorization, retry and auditing stay with the runtime. Forgetting who executes is the most expensive mistake that shows up in production.

sections.1.body.0.t: Each tool is declared to the model by a JSON schema with name, description and typed parameters. The LLM uses this schema as a grammar: it knows the name, knows the format of the arguments and uses the description to decide when it makes sense to call.

sections.1.body.1.t: The description is the most neglected part. The LLM does not read code: it reads the string. 'Gets the weather for a city' is better than 'get_weather', because the model decides when to call based on prose. Schemas with poor descriptions lead the model to call the tool at the wrong time, or not to call it at all.

sections.2.body.0.t: When the model returns a function call, the runtime receives a JSON that may be wrong: wrong type, missing field, value outside the enum, string where a number should be. Validating before executing is non-negotiable: it is the boundary between the model, which proposes, and your code, which executes with real permissions.

sections.2.body.1.t: In Python, Pydantic is the standard path: declare a model, call model_validate(model_dump), and Pydantic raises ValidationError with the exact list of fields and the reason. In TypeScript, the natural pair is Zod, with safeParse returning { success, data, error }.

sections.3.body.0.t: A tool call goes through five stages, each with a possible response and a distinct error path. Without seeing all five it looks like magic, and the bugs stay hidden.

sections.3.body.1.t: 1. declaration: the list of schemas is handed to the LLM along with the prompt.

sections.3.body.2.t: 2. proposal: the LLM returns tool_calls with name + JSON arguments.

sections.3.body.3.t: 3. validation: the runtime parses and validates against the schema; a failure here means 'the model hallucinated'; treat it as an error and return the reason to the LLM.

sections.3.body.4.t: 4. execution: the runtime calls the real function (HTTP, DB, command) with permissions and a timeout.

sections.3.body.5.t: 5. observation: the result becomes a tool message in the context; the LLM uses it for the next decision.

sections.3.heading.t: The complete flow, end to end

sections.4.bullets.0.t: the model can invent fields: it has seen 1000 different schemas and does not guarantee consistency

sections.4.bullets.1.t: types are guaranteed, values are not: it knows 'unit' is a string, but may send 'celcius' (misspelled)

sections.4.bullets.2.t: enums are the most common error boundary: the model does not always respect the enum, especially without strict structured output

sections.4.bullets.3.t: validation is cheap: it costs microseconds; executing without validation can trigger a critical action with wrong arguments

sections.5.bullets.0.t: strength: the schema forces structure; the model does not need to 'try' to produce valid JSON; it is producing tokens within a grammar

sections.5.bullets.1.t: strength: validation errors return a rich message to the model, which almost always corrects itself on the next turn

sections.5.bullets.2.t: weak: a poor description leads to calls at the wrong time; writing a good schema is design work

sections.5.bullets.3.t: weakness: the call is opaque to the user; if they do not read the trace, they do not know which tool ran

sections.5.bullets.4.t: weakness: parallelism depends on the provider; some allow several tool_calls in one response, others only one

short.t: the model invokes typed external functions

tagline.t: Tool calling is the contract between the LLM and the world: the model returns structured JSON (name + arguments), the runtime validates it against a schema and executes. It is what turns text into action.
